---
title: "2. Quarto Flow"
subtitle: "Two files, one workflow: analysis.qmd and index.qmd"
---

The heart of this workflow is a two-file Quarto structure. Most tutorials use a single `.qmd` file for everything, but separating your analysis from your manuscript gives you the best of both worlds: a clean, readable paper and a fully transparent, reproducible analysis.

## Why two files?

| | `analysis.qmd` | `index.qmd` |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Reproducible analytical record | Clean journal manuscript |
| **Contains** | All R code, models, figures, tables | Text only, figure references |
| **Who reads it** | Reviewers, other researchers | Journal editors, readers |
| **Renders to** | HTML (best for code display) | PDF or Word (for submission) |
| **Tone** | Code-heavy, annotated | Academic prose |

Both files are version controlled together on GitHub. Together they give the complete picture of your research.

## How they connect

`analysis.qmd` runs all your R code and saves figures and derived data to the `outputs/` folder. `index.qmd` references those saved files.

```
analysis.qmd  →  runs R code  →  saves to outputs/figures/
                                                   ↓
index.qmd     →  references figure  →  manuscript PDF
```

This means:
- Changing your analysis in `analysis.qmd` automatically updates the figures in `index.qmd` when you re-render
- Your manuscript stays clean — no R code chunks in the middle of your methods section
- A reviewer can open `analysis.qmd` and see every modelling decision you made

## Structure of analysis.qmd

```{.quarto}
---
title: "Analysis: Kōura habitat preference study"
format: html
execute:
  echo: true        # show all code
  warning: false
  message: false
---

## Setup

```{{r}}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(ggplot2)

# Load derived data
data <- read_csv("data/derived/koura_data.csv")
```

## Data cleaning

```{{r}}
#| label: data-cleaning

# Remove incomplete observations
data_clean <- data |>
  filter(!is.na(shelter_type)) |>
  mutate(size_class = cut(carapace_length_mm, 
                          breaks = c(0, 20, 35, Inf),
                          labels = c("juvenile", "sub-adult", "adult")))

# Save derived data
write_csv(data_clean, "data/derived/koura_clean.csv")
```

## Statistical models

```{{r}}
#| label: model-preference
#| cache: true

model_preference <- brm(
  shelter_choice ~ size_class + (1|tank_id),
  data = data_clean,
  family = categorical(),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 4000
)

saveRDS(model_preference, "outputs/model_preference.rds")
```

## Figures

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-preference
#| fig-cap: "Kōura shelter preference by size class"

fig_preference <- ggplot(data_clean, 
                         aes(x = shelter_type, 
                             fill = size_class)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2E7D6B", "#4CAF93", "#A8D5C8")) +
  labs(x = "Shelter type", 
       y = "Count",
       fill = "Size class") +
  theme_minimal()

# Save for use in manuscript
ggsave("outputs/figures/fig-preference.png", 
       fig_preference, 
       width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

fig_preference
```
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### Use `#| cache: true` for slow models
Bayesian models can take minutes or hours to run. Adding `#| cache: true` to those chunks means Quarto saves the result and skips re-running on the next render unless the code changes. Combined with `saveRDS()`, this makes your workflow fast even with complex models.
:::

format:

    documentclass: article
    linestretch: 2
  docx:

bibliography: references/references.bib
csl: references/aquatic-conservation.csl

## Rendering both files

In Positron, you can render each file independently:

- Click **Render** in the top bar when `analysis.qmd` is open → generates HTML with all your code and outputs
- Click **Render** when `index.qmd` is open → generates your PDF manuscript

**Always render `analysis.qmd` first** if you have changed any code, so the figures in `outputs/figures/` are up to date before the manuscript renders.

::: {.callout-note}
### Placeholder data example
The code examples on this page use realistic but placeholder kōura data. The actual data structure used in published kōura mesocosm studies includes columns for `shelter_type`, `carapace_length_mm`, `tank_id`, `round`, and `sex`. If you are adapting this for your own species, adjust the variable names accordingly.
:::

## Session info and reproducibility

At the end of your `analysis.qmd`, always include:

```r
#| label: session-info
sessionInfo()
```

This prints all package versions in your rendered HTML — a second line of defence alongside `renv.lock` for anyone trying to reproduce your work.
